newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia calls on ASEAN to help prevent new war.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia calls on ASEAN to help prevent new war.

text.p: Cambodia called on the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Saturday to help prevent a new war in Cambodia and told opposition politicians to give up their resistance to the new government in Phnom Penh.

The government said in a statement, released as strongman Hun Sen entered talks with an ASEAN mediation team, that it was able to resolve its internal problems on its own but welcomed ASEAN's contribution to peace and stability in the country.
"The royal government of Cambodia welcomes the intention of the ASEAN countries to contribute to the stability and peace in Cambodia through constructive consultation," the statement said.
"One important contribution that ASEAN could offer is not to encourage any new war in Cambodia," the statement said.
Cambodia has been in turmoil since Second Prime Minster Hun Sen ousted his senior co-premier, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, on July 6 after two days of battles in Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen subsequently rejected attempts to mediate in the crisis and warned against any interference by outside powers in Cambodia's affairs.

The ASEAN team meeting Hun Sen on Saturday is made up of the same men who tried unsuccessfully to launch a mediation effort two weeks ago -- foreign ministers Ali Alatas of Indonesia, Prachuab Chaiyasan of Thailand and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines.
Forces loyal to the rival prime ministers have clashed intermittently in parts of north and northwest Cambodia since the prince's ouster.

Saturday's government statement called on Ranariddh, who left Cambodia shortly before Hun Sen's takeover, to cease his fight against the government and stop collaborating with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group.

"The royal government deems it necessary that Norodom Ranariddh ceases immediately his war...(by) ceasing completely and definitely the political and military collaboration with the outlawed Khmer Rouge," the statement said.

"The only option for any political party or individual who wishes to participate in the political life in Cambodia is to abandon completely and definitely the military activity against the government."

Ranariddh was negotiating with the Khmer Rouge before his ouster and the guerrillas, who purged their notorious leader Pol Pot last week, have said they support Ranariddh and have vowed to unite with all anti-Hun Sen forces and "destroy" his government.

A Khmer Rouge military commander told the Far Eastern Economic Review in a report published on Thursday that Pol Pot, responsible for the death of more than a million people during his 1975-79 rule, was purged because of his opposition to an alliance with the royalists.
Hun Sen has threatened military action against the Khmer Rouge and said Pol Pot must be tried by an international court.

In the Saturday statement the Cambodian government said it welcomed the "just position" taken by Thailand towards Cambodia, in particular "its refusal to offer any support and permission to use Thai territory for an armed struggle infiltrating Cambodia".

Cambodia also called on Thailand to encourage opposition politicians who fled to Bangkok in the aftermath of Ranariddh's ouster and a crackdown against his royalist party, to return to Cambodia and resume their political activities.

The statement made no mention of Ranariddh's return. Hun Sen has said the prince was free go home but he would have to face trial for his illegal negotiations with the outlawed Khmer Rouge and for alleged weapons smuggling.
The statement said the government would reinstate royalist soldiers who returned to the government side with the exception of the most senior commanders.

The government was committed to holding a May 1998 election on schedule and was confident in its capacity to organise and hold the poll but it would welcome international observers and a United Nations coordinating role, the statement said.
